significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish that numeral-system transparency predicts both the linearity of multilingual models’ magnitude representations and arithmetic error, while failure to map word numerals onto a shared "digit-magnitude representation" causally mediates that relationship; this is a form-(iii) predictive coupling supplemented by a form-(ii) mechanism. It would establish both a behavioral phenomenon and a mechanism, fixing expectations for untested numeral systems and explaining a specific component of the cross-language performance variation measured by work such as MGSM (Shi et al., 2023), rather than merely showing that numeric magnitude is decodable as in prior numeracy probing. The branches are determinate and both informative: refutation would support the claim’s explicit alternative that "models fully normalize word-forms to a shared representation" and rule out numeral grammar as an explanation for these arithmetic gaps, although the conclusion remains bounded to numeral-word arithmetic. In the topic-substitution check, deleting the transparency–distortion–error relation leaves only the generic shared-versus-language-specific representation question and would not earn this score, so the increment is genuinely claim-specific.

reach.justification: The claim hands over three named handles: a quantitative "numeral transparency score," the design rule of "transliterating word-form numbers to digits," and "internal steering that injects the shared digit-magnitude representation." The transparency score is an ex-ante predictor and digit conversion is an ex-ante intervention with an action window before arithmetic errors, making them potentially useful to practitioners building or auditing multilingual numeric interfaces rather than only to mechanistic-interpretability researchers. The hypothesized transparency–linearity–error relation predicts what should be found after measurements are re-extracted on another multilingual model or extended to another numeral system, whereas the internal steering vector and layer location would require model-specific rediscovery; scope is consequently broad across languages and multilingual model families but narrow to number-word processing and arithmetic. The topic-substitution check removes all of these handles and leaves no comparable forecast or deployment rule, so the reach comes from this claim rather than from multilingual interpretability generally.
